rationale: Start with a broad mid-strength scouting gradient at moderate temperature to spread unknown compounds across the run while encouraging all 10 to elute. This should give a first map of retention range and crowding to guide subsequent optimization.

All compounds eluted early with perfect resolution, so the main opportunity is to reduce the time penalty by lowering the final organic strength while keeping the same gradient length and temperature. This should retain late-eluting compounds a bit longer without risking loss of any peaks, and may improve packing of the chromatogram toward a higher CRF.

The first run already had full elution and ample resolution, so the best path is to shorten the gradient to cut analysis time while checking whether the closest cluster around peaks 5–7 remains acceptably resolved. Keeping phi0, phi1, and temperature fixed isolates the effect of gradient steepness cleanly.

The 10 min gradient is very fast but slightly under-resolves the critical pair, while 20 min fully resolves everything with extra time cost. A 12 min gradient should be a near-optimal compromise, restoring the critical resolution with only a small increase in run time.

The trend suggests the critical pair improves steadily as tG increases, and the current method still has no time penalty. Testing 14 min should determine whether a small extra increase in gradient time pushes the minimum resolution into the optimal region and raises CRF further.

CRF is now very near the maximum, and the only unresolved question is whether a slightly longer gradient moves the critical pair into the best-resolution window without yet incurring a time penalty. Testing 16 min is the smallest logical step to check if the optimum lies just above 14 min.

Since 14 min is near-optimal but the critical pair is still just under the apparent target, a small reduction in final organic strength may selectively expand the later crowded region without adding enough retention to trigger a time penalty. This tests whether composition can improve the 14 min method beyond the current best.

The optimum has been reached, so this run is only to probe local robustness around the best point. Lowering phi1 one step tests whether the maximum is broad or sharply tuned while likely keeping all compounds eluting within the no-penalty window.

You already have a perfect-scoring method, so this run can map robustness in an orthogonal direction. Lowering temperature may slightly increase selectivity around the critical mid-run cluster while showing whether the optimum is stable to a 5 C shift.

The lower-temperature test worsened selectivity and shifted the critical overlap, so the opposite temperature direction is the most informative orthogonal robustness check. Raising T by 5 C may smooth the mid-cluster differently and reveal whether the perfect point at 40 C is a local maximum or part of a broader plateau.

With the optimum already found, this run probes whether the perfect score depends mainly on the final strength or also on the starting strength. Lowering phi0 may expand early gradient space and subtly redistribute the crowded mid-run region while likely preserving full elution and zero time penalty.

The lower-phi0 test increased retention and slightly reduced CRF, so the complementary direction can define sensitivity to the starting composition. Raising phi0 one step should compress the early region and may reveal whether the perfect optimum is robust to a modestly stronger initial mobile phase.

A second distinct method has now achieved the maximum CRF, so the best use of another run is to explore whether the optimum extends further in the stronger-start direction. This will help identify a broader robust operating window around the perfect-scoring region.

Both 0.10/0.85 and 0.15/0.85 give perfect CRF, so this run checks whether slightly stronger final organic can preserve the maximum when paired with the stronger starting composition. It helps map the 2D plateau of optimal methods rather than just isolated points.

The perfect region appears centered near phi1 = 0.85 with phi0 between 0.10 and 0.15, so testing one step lower in phi1 at the other perfect phi0 point is the most informative remaining local check. This will define whether the optimum plateau extends symmetrically or if 0.85 is the clear center.

Most of the local grid around the optimum has been sampled except the low-phi0/high-phi1 corner. Testing 0.05/0.90 completes that neighborhood and clarifies whether the perfect plateau is bounded mainly by phi0, phi1, or both.

This fills the remaining stronger-start/lower-end corner adjacent to the optimal region and helps define the full local response surface. It is likely still safe for full elution while showing whether the CRF loss at higher phi0 is driven by phi0 alone or by interaction with phi1.

The perfect-scoring plateau now clearly extends to phi0 = 0.20 and phi1 = 0.80, so pushing phi0 one more step higher is the most efficient way to locate the upper boundary. This should show whether the optimum window can be widened further or if early compression starts to hurt the critical pair.

Since phi0 = 0.25 crossed the boundary due to early peak compression, the next useful boundary check is to keep phi0 at the highest perfect value and reduce phi1 one step. This tests whether the plateau around phi0 = 0.20 extends further to lower final strength without losing the optimum.

The remaining immediate local point around the strongest perfect-start condition is the higher phi1 corner. Running 0.20/0.90 will complete the local map and determine whether the perfect plateau includes this combination or if phi1 above 0.85 starts to erode the critical pair.

Most boundaries of the 14 min, 40 C optimum plateau are mapped except the low-phi0/low-phi1 corner. This run completes that corner and helps define the full robust operating window among the already near-optimal conditions.

The perfect region appears to span phi0 about 0.10–0.20 and phi1 about 0.80–0.85, but the intermediate point at 0.15/0.75 has not been tested. This run checks whether the lower phi1 boundary dips inward or remains flat through the center of the robust window.

With several perfect methods already identified at 14 min, a final useful question is whether one of them can be shortened while preserving the maximum score. Testing the best-known composition at 12 min checks if the 14 min optimum sits on a broad time plateau or at the minimum gradient time needed for CRF 1.000.

Since 0.20/0.80 is also a perfect 14 min method, checking it at 12 min tests whether a stronger starting composition better preserves the critical pair under a shorter gradient. This is the most plausible remaining route to a shorter maximum-scoring method.

With the maximum CRF already achieved, the final run should probe the other side of the time optimum for the central perfect method. This confirms whether the perfect region is narrowly pinned to 14 min or remains robust with slightly longer gradient time before the time penalty appears.
